Pattern 01 of 24

Prefix Sum

Do the adding once up front, so that any "sum of a range" question later becomes a single subtraction.

1. What is this pattern for?

Think of a car's odometer. You don't measure how far you drove today with a tape measure. You read the odometer tonight, subtract this morning's reading, and you're done.

A prefix sum array stores a running total. prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers. After building it once in O(n), the sum of any slice nums[l..r] comes from one subtraction in O(1):

# The one formula to remember (prefix has a leading 0):
#   sum of nums[left..right], both ends included, = prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]
def slice_sum(prefix, left, right):
    # odometer reading "after right" minus odometer reading "before left"
    return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]

It's for problems that keep asking about totals over contiguous ranges (subarrays, or sub-rectangles in a grid), especially when there are many such questions or you'd otherwise need two nested loops.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Pad with a zero. Make prefix one longer than nums and set prefix[0] = 0. That zero means "sum of nothing", and it removes every edge case at index 0.
  2. Accumulate. prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + nums[i]. Each cell is the odometer reading after visiting element i.
  3. Subtract to answer. Range [l, r] = reading after r minus reading before l = prefix[r+1] - prefix[l].
  4. Level up: prefix + hash map. To count subarrays with sum k, walk once and ask: "Have I seen a running total of current - k before?" If so, the slice between that earlier point and now sums to k.

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Prefix Sum

Trigger words

  • "sum of subarray", "range sum", "between index i and j"
  • "number of subarrays whose sum equals / is divisible by k"
  • "equal number of 0s and 1s" (map 0 to −1, then look for sum 0)
  • "many queries" on an array that doesn't change
  • "sub-matrix sum", "region sum" in a grid

Shape of the input

  • An array or grid of numbers, possibly negative. Negatives break Sliding Window but not Prefix Sum.
  • The answer depends on a contiguous slice.
  • The brute force is "for every l, for every r, add up". That's O(n²) or O(n³).
The one question to ask"Could I answer this if I knew the total up to every index?" If yes, it's Prefix Sum.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use Prefix Sum when…Prefer something else when…
There are many range-sum queries on a static arrayThe array changes between queries: use a Fenwick / Segment tree
You're counting subarrays with sum = k, and values can be negativeAll values are positive and you want the longest/shortest window: use Sliding Window, which uses O(1) space
"Equal count" problems that become "sum = 0" after a mappingYou need a max/min over a range, not a sum: use a sparse table or Monotonic Stack
Sub-rectangle sums in a grid (2-D prefix)The operation can't be undone by subtraction (max, gcd…)

Cost: build O(n) time and O(n) space; each query O(1). The prefix + hash map version is O(n) time and O(n) space.

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

Prefix Sum has two templates. They share one idea, a running total ("odometer reading") at every point, but answer different questions. Template A keeps every reading so it can answer many range-sum questions instantly. Template B keeps a logbook of readings it has passed, to count how many slices add up to exactly k. Read each one in order: question → hook → story → code → watch it run → invariant.

Template A · Build prefix sums, then answer range sums in O(1)

The question it answersWhat is the sum of nums[left..right]? (asked many times)
What it keepsEvery odometer reading: prefix[i] = sum of the first i numbers.
When it checks for an answerAfter the build, each query is one subtraction.
Use it whenThe array doesn't change and there are many range-sum queries.
Not forCounting slices with a target sum (Template B), or arrays that change between queries (a Fenwick tree, page 24).
Memory hook: "Reading after the end minus reading before the start"Drive the array once, writing down the odometer at every checkpoint. The distance of any stretch is the reading after its last leg minus the reading before its first leg.

The story, mapped to the code. Each number is one leg of a trip. The car starts at the factory with the odometer at 0.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
The factory reading before any drivingprefix[0] = 0The total of nothing; it lets a stretch starting at index 0 have a "before" reading.
One leg of the tripnums[i]The distance added at step i.
Reading before leg iprefix[i]Sum of nums[0..i-1].
Reading after leg iprefix[i + 1]Sum of nums[0..i]: the reading before plus this leg.
Distance of the stretch left..rightprefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]Reading after leg right, minus reading before leg left.

The template. Two small functions: build once, then query as often as you like. The extra slot at the front is the factory reading.

def build_prefix(nums):
    prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        number = nums[i]
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + number
    return prefix


def range_sum(prefix, left, right):
    return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]
function buildPrefix(nums: number[]): number[] {
  const prefix: number[] = new Array(nums.length + 1).fill(0);
  for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    const number = nums[i];
    prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + number;
  }
  return prefix;
}

function rangeSum(prefix: number[], left: number, right: number): number {
  return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left];
}
static int[] buildPrefix(int[] nums) {
    int[] prefix = new int[nums.length + 1];
    for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        int number = nums[i];
        prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + number;
    }
    return prefix;
}

static int rangeSum(int[] prefix, int left, int right) {
    return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left];
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
prefix = [0] * (len(nums) + 1)Makes one slot per checkpoint: n numbers have n + 1 readings, from the factory to the end.Write the factory reading, 0, in slot 0.Without the extra slot, a range starting at index 0 has no "before" reading and needs a special case.
for i in range(len(nums))Visits each leg once, left to right.Drive the trip in order.Readings depend on the previous one, so the order can't change.
number = nums[i]Reads this leg's distance.Look at the next leg.Only for readability.
prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + numberReading after leg i = reading before leg i + the leg.The odometer goes up by this leg.Writing to prefix[i] instead shifts every reading by one: the classic off-by-one.
return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]Range sum in one subtraction.Reading after the last leg minus reading before the first leg.prefix[right] - prefix[left] drops the last number; prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left + 1] drops the first.

Watch it run. Step through the build, then a query for left = 1, right = 3. Switch the code language at the top; the trace is the same. Tick Predict each step to guess the next reading before it appears.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. After processing index i, prefix[i + 1] equals nums[0] + … + nums[i], and every earlier slot is already final. So any range sum is the difference of two finished readings.

Complexity. Build: O(n) time, O(n) extra space for the readings. Each query: O(1) time. Worth it once there are more than a couple of queries.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Forgetting the leading 0. "The factory reading" is part of the hook: without it, ranges starting at 0 break.
  • prefix[right] - prefix[left]. Say "reading after right" and the + 1 writes itself.
  • Building inside every query. You drive the trip once; queries only read the log.
Recall card
Memory hook
Reading after the end minus reading before the start.
Choose this template when
Static array, many "sum of this range" questions → build once, subtract per query.
Invariant
prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers.
The line people get wrong
prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]: the + 1 belongs to the right end only.

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

Why does prefix have n + 1 slots?

Because there are n + 1 readings: the factory reading 0, then one after each of the n legs.

With prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14], what is nums[2..4]?

prefix[5] − prefix[2] = 14 − 4 = 10 (that's 4 + 1 + 5).

What does prefix[3] mean in words?

The total of the first three numbers, nums[0..2]: the reading before leg 3.

Template B · Count subarrays whose sum is exactly k (works with negatives)

The question it answersHow many contiguous slices add up to exactly k?
What it keepsA logbook seen: each running total reached so far → how many times.
When it checks for an answerAt every index, before logging the current reading.
Use it whenCounting (or finding) slices with a target sum, especially when numbers can be negative, so a sliding window can't work.
Not forMany range-sum queries (Template A); "longest/shortest slice" questions need first/last positions instead of counts.
Memory hook: "Which earlier reading would make this stretch exactly k?"At each point, ask the logbook how many times you've passed the reading running − k. Each of those earlier points starts a stretch ending here that is exactly k long. Then log where you are now.

The story, mapped to the code. Same trip, but you don't keep a reading for every checkpoint. You keep a logbook that counts how often each reading has appeared. Negative numbers just mean the meter goes down for a leg; nothing else changes.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Current meter readingrunningSum of everything so far.
The stretch length we wantkTarget sum of a slice.
The earlier reading that would make it workneeded = running - kIf we passed this reading before, the stretch since then is exactly k.
Logbook of readings passedseenRunning total → how many times we've been there.
The factory reading, already in the logbookseen = {0: 1}Lets a stretch that starts at index 0 be counted.
Stretches found so farcountThe answer.

The template. Five steps per number, always in this order: add, compute the needed reading, look it up, count, then log.

def count_subarrays(nums, k):
    seen = {0: 1}
    running = 0
    count = 0
    for number in nums:
        running += number
        needed = running - k
        if needed in seen:
            count += seen[needed]
        seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1
    return count
function countSubarrays(nums: number[], k: number): number {
  const seen = new Map<number, number>([[0, 1]]);
  let running = 0;
  let count = 0;
  for (const number of nums) {
    running += number;
    const needed = running - k;
    if (seen.has(needed)) {
      count += seen.get(needed)!;
    }
    seen.set(running, (seen.get(running) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  return count;
}
static int countSubarrays(int[] nums, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
    seen.put(0, 1);
    int running = 0;
    int count = 0;
    for (int number : nums) {
        running += number;
        int needed = running - k;
        if (seen.containsKey(needed)) {
            count += seen.get(needed);
        }
        seen.merge(running, 1, Integer::sum);
    }
    return count;
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves
seen = {0: 1}Logs the reading 0 once, before any number.The factory reading is already in the logbook.Without it, a slice starting at index 0 (like nums[0..1] here) is never counted.
running += numberMoves the meter by this number (down, if it's negative).Drive the next leg.Must come first: everything after uses the new reading.
needed = running - kThe earlier reading that would make the stretch since then exactly k."Where would I have had to be?"Writing k - running flips the sign and finds the wrong readings.
if needed in seen: count += seen[needed]Adds one stretch for every time we passed that reading.Count the matching log entries.Adding 1 instead of seen[needed] undercounts when a reading repeats (zeros or negatives).
seen[running] = seen.get(running, 0) + 1Logs the current reading for future positions.Write today's reading in the logbook.Doing this before the lookup lets the current reading match itself when k = 0: an empty slice gets counted. See the second player.

Watch it run. Step through nums = [1, 1, 1], k = 2. Tick Predict each step to guess needed and the count before they appear. The second player shows why the lookup must come before the logging.

With k = 0, logging first makes every reading match itself, counting empty slices: 5 instead of the correct 2 ([1, −1] and [−1, 1]).

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. When we reach index i, seen holds the readings of every prefix that ends before i (including the empty prefix). So seen[running − k] counts exactly the slices that end at i and sum to k.

Complexity. O(n) time: one pass with O(1) dictionary operations. O(n) extra space: up to n + 1 different readings in the logbook.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Logging before looking up. The hook's order is "ask, then log": you can only ask about readings you passed before now.
  • Forgetting seen = {0: 1}. The factory reading is in the logbook from the start.
  • Using a sliding window. With negative numbers the meter goes down, so shrinking a window doesn't reliably reduce the sum. The logbook doesn't care.
  • Storing positions instead of counts. Counting needs how many times; "longest slice" problems store the first position instead.
Recall card
Memory hook
Which earlier reading would make this stretch exactly k? Ask the logbook, then log.
Choose this template when
"Count/find slices with sum (or a property) equal to k", especially with negatives → running total + logbook of counts.
Invariant
seen holds every reading strictly before the current index, with the empty prefix as 0.
The line people get wrong
Recording seen[running] must come after the lookup.

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

Why is seen started as {0: 1}?

It's the reading before any number; it lets slices starting at index 0 be found (needed = 0).

At running = 7 with k = 3, which key do you look up?

needed = 7 − 3 = 4.

Why add seen[needed] rather than 1?

Each earlier time we passed that reading starts a different valid slice; readings can repeat when numbers are zero or negative.

Choosing between the templates

QuestionTemplate ATemplate B
Main purposeAnswer many range-sum queriesCount slices whose sum is exactly k
Information keptEvery reading, by position (prefix list)How often each reading occurred (seen map)
Meaning of the running totalprefix[i] = sum before index irunning = sum through the current index
Why a hash map?Not needed: queries ask for positions, which index the listNeeded: we look up by value ("have I passed reading X?")
When the answer is computedLater, per queryDuring the single pass, before logging
Typical prompt"Sum of elements between i and j" (LC 303)"Number of subarrays with sum k" (LC 560)
TimeO(n) build + O(1) per queryO(n)
SpaceO(n)O(n)

Both rest on "a stretch = later reading minus earlier reading". A fixes the stretch's ends and looks up readings by position; B fixes the stretch's length (k) and looks up readings by value. Pick by the question: "sum of this range?" → A; "how many ranges sum to k?" → B.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Odometer minus odometer"Sum between two points = reading at the end minus reading at the start. Pad with a 0, like the car leaving the factory.
How this hook works: what “Odometer minus odometer” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Odometer”
The running total. prefix[i] is the odometer reading after driving past the first i numbers. It only ever adds, like a car's distance meter.
“minus odometer”
Any stretch is the difference of two readings: the reading at the end minus the reading at the start. You never re-add the numbers in between.
“Pad with a 0”
A new car leaves the factory reading 0. prefix[0] = 0 is that reading, so a stretch that starts at index 0 still has a "start reading" to subtract.

Why this picture fits the pattern: Prefix-sum problems keep asking "what is the total between here and there?" That is exactly the question an odometer answers with one subtraction, after you've done the driving once.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
One leg of the tripnums[i]
Odometer reading after leg iprefix[i + 1]
The factory readingprefix[0] = 0
Trip from leg l to leg rprefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]
A logbook of readings you've passedseen (running total → how many times)

Watch it on numbers

nums = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5], so the readings are prefix = [0, 3, 4, 8, 9, 14]. What is nums[1..3]?

  1. Reading after leg 3 is prefix[4] = 9.
  2. Reading before leg 1 is prefix[1] = 3.
  3. Trip distance = 9 − 3 = 6, and indeed 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.
  4. The whole array: prefix[5] - prefix[0] = 14 − 0 = 14. The padded 0 makes this work without a special case.

The trap it saves you from

The off-by-one in prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l]. Say it as "reading after r minus reading before l" and the + 1 writes itself. Forgetting the 0 pad breaks every slice that starts at index 0.

It still works when…

Counting subarrays that sum to k (LeetCode 560): at each reading running, ask "did I pass the reading running - k earlier?" If the odometer said 1 and now says 3, that stretch was 2 km. On [1, 1, 1] with k = 2 the readings are 1, 2, 3: at 2 we passed 0 once, at 3 we passed 1 once, so the answer is 2.

Picture

A staircase where each step's height is the running total. Any slice's sum is the height difference between two steps.

Chant

"Pad zero, run total, right plus one minus left."

Hash-map twist

"What did I need to have seen?" → running − k. Store totals, not indices, when you're counting.

Each template, in the hook's words

Template (section 5)In the hook's wordsThe line that does it
A · Build prefix sumsDrive once and write down every odometer reading, starting from the factory 0.prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + number
A · Range sumAny stretch is the reading at its end minus the reading before its start.prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left]
B · Count sums equal to kAt each reading, ask how many earlier readings were exactly k less. Keep a tally of readings seen.count += seen[running - k]

Medium 560. Subarray Sum Equals K Start here Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft Apple ArrayHash Map

Problem: Given nums (can contain negatives) and k, return how many contiguous subarrays sum to k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,1,1], k = 2
Output: 2
Example 2
Input: nums = [1,2,3], k = 3
Output: 2

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · -1000 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 1000 · -10⁷ ≤ k ≤ 10⁷

Hint 1

The sum of nums[i..j] equals prefix[j + 1] − prefix[i]. If that difference must be k, what earlier prefix are you looking for?

Hint 2

Walk once, keeping a running sum. Count how many earlier prefixes equal running − k; a dictionary of prefix → how many times seen answers that instantly.

From brute force to the pattern: Try every start i and every end j and add up the slice: O(n³), or O(n²) if you extend a running sum from each start. The waste is that every slice sum is rebuilt from scratch. With prefix sums a slice sum is one subtraction, and storing the prefixes you've seen in a hash map turns "is there a start that makes this sum k?" into one O(1) lookup, so the whole thing is O(n).

Spot it: "number of subarrays" + "sum equals k" + negatives allowed, so Sliding Window won't work. That points to Prefix Sum + hash map.

Key insight: If running_now − running_earlier = k, then the slice between those two points sums to k. So at every step, count how many earlier prefixes equal running_now − k.

Approach:

  1. Seed seen = {0: 1} for the empty prefix.
  2. For each number, add it to running.
  3. Add seen[running − k] to the count: each one is a start point that makes a k-sum slice ending here.
  4. Only then record running in seen.
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def subarraySum(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        # seen: running total -> how many times we have reached that total so far
        seen = {}
        # The empty prefix (before index 0) has total 0. Recording it lets
        # a slice that starts at index 0 be counted.
        seen[0] = 1
        running = 0   # sum of nums[0..i]
        count = 0     # the answer
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            number = nums[i]
            running = running + number
            # A slice ending at i sums to k exactly when an earlier running
            # total equals running - k. Count all such earlier totals.
            needed = running - k
            if needed in seen:
                count = count + seen[needed]
            # Record AFTER counting, so we never count an empty slice.
            if running not in seen:
                seen[running] = 0
            seen[running] = seen[running] + 1
        return count
function subarraySum(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    // seen: running total -> how many times we have reached that total so far
    const seen = new Map<number, number>();
    // The empty prefix (before index 0) has total 0. Recording it lets
    // a slice that starts at index 0 be counted.
    seen.set(0, 1);
    let running = 0;   // sum of nums[0..i]
    let count = 0;     // the answer
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const number = nums[i];
        running = running + number;
        // A slice ending at i sums to k exactly when an earlier running
        // total equals running - k. Count all such earlier totals.
        const needed = running - k;
        if (seen.has(needed)) {
            count = count + seen.get(needed)!;
        }
        // Record AFTER counting, so we never count an empty slice.
        seen.set(running, (seen.get(running) ?? 0) + 1);
    }
    return count;
}
class Solution {
    public int subarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // seen: running total -> how many times we have reached that total so far
        Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
        // The empty prefix (before index 0) has total 0. Recording it lets
        // a slice that starts at index 0 be counted.
        seen.put(0, 1);
        int running = 0;   // sum of nums[0..i]
        int count = 0;     // the answer
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int number = nums[i];
            running = running + number;
            // A slice ending at i sums to k exactly when an earlier running
            // total equals running - k. Count all such earlier totals.
            int needed = running - k;
            if (seen.containsKey(needed)) {
                count = count + seen.get(needed);
            }
            // Record AFTER counting, so we never count an empty slice.
            seen.put(running, seen.getOrDefault(running, 0) + 1);
        }
        return count;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. seen is a dictionary from "running total" to "how many times we reached it". We seed it with seen[0] = 1 for the empty prefix.
  2. running is the sum of everything up to the current index; count is the answer.
  3. In the loop, we read nums[i] into number and add it to running.
  4. needed = running - k: if some earlier running total equals this, the slice after that point up to i sums to k. We add how many times we saw it.
  5. Finally we record running in seen (create it with 0 if new, then add 1). This happens after counting, so a slice never pairs with itself.
  6. After the loop, count holds the number of slices that sum to k.

Dry run on the example nums = [1, 2, 3], k = 3:

inumberrunningneededaddedcountseen after
011-200{0: 1, 1: 1}
123011{0: 1, 1: 1, 3: 1}
236312{0: 1, 1: 1, 3: 1, 6: 1}

Result: 2. The two slices are [1, 2] (found at i = 1, because total 0 was seen) and [3] (found at i = 2, because total 3 was seen).

Edge cases to test:

  • k = 0 with zeros in the array, e.g. [0, 0, 0] → 6 subarrays (forgetting to seed {0: 1} gives the wrong count).
  • Negative numbers, e.g. [1, -1, 0], k = 0: a sliding window would fail here, prefix sums don't.
  • A single element equal to k, e.g. [3], k = 3 → 1.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 525. Contiguous Array Google Meta Amazon Cisco Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: In a binary array, find the length of the longest subarray with an equal number of 0s and 1s.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [0,1]
Output: 2
Explanation: [0, 1] is the longest contiguous subarray with an equal number of 0 and 1.
Example 2
Input: nums = [0,1,0]
Output: 2
Explanation: [0, 1] (or [1, 0]) is a longest contiguous subarray with equal number of 0 and 1.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · nums[i] is either 0 or 1.

Hint 1

Replace every 0 with −1. What does "equal number of 0s and 1s" become in terms of the sum?

Hint 2

A subarray with sum 0 sits between two equal prefix sums. To get the longest, remember the first index each prefix sum appeared.

From brute force to the pattern: Check every subarray and count its 0s and 1s: O(n²). Mapping 0 → −1 turns "balanced" into "sums to 0", and two equal prefix sums enclose such a subarray. Storing the first index of each prefix sum lets you measure the longest one in a single O(n) pass.

Spot it: "equal number of" → turn each 0 into −1. Now "equal" means "sum is 0". It's a longest question, so store the first index where each running sum appears.

Approach:

  1. Map 0 → −1 and 1 → +1, so "equal counts" means "sum 0".
  2. Store the first index at which each running sum appears, seeded with {0: -1}.
  3. When a running sum repeats, the slice between the two indices sums to 0. Update the best length.
class Solution:
    def findMaxLength(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # first_at: running sum -> the FIRST index where we saw it
        first_at = {}
        # Running sum 0 is "seen" just before index 0 (at index -1).
        first_at[0] = -1
        running = 0   # (number of 1s) - (number of 0s) so far
        best = 0      # longest balanced slice found so far
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            bit = nums[i]
            # Treat 1 as +1 and 0 as -1, so "equal counts" means "sum is 0".
            if bit == 1:
                running = running + 1
            else:
                running = running - 1
            if running in first_at:
                # Same running sum as at index first_at[running]: the slice
                # after that index, up to i, has sum 0, so it is balanced.
                length = i - first_at[running]
                if length > best:
                    best = length
            else:
                # First time we see this sum: remember where. Never overwrite
                # it, because the earliest index gives the longest slice.
                first_at[running] = i
        return best
function findMaxLength(nums: number[]): number {
    // firstAt: running sum -> the FIRST index where we saw it
    const firstAt = new Map<number, number>();
    // Running sum 0 is "seen" just before index 0 (at index -1).
    firstAt.set(0, -1);
    let running = 0;   // (number of 1s) - (number of 0s) so far
    let best = 0;      // longest balanced slice found so far
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const bit = nums[i];
        // Treat 1 as +1 and 0 as -1, so "equal counts" means "sum is 0".
        if (bit === 1) {
            running = running + 1;
        } else {
            running = running - 1;
        }
        if (firstAt.has(running)) {
            // Same running sum as at index firstAt[running]: the slice
            // after that index, up to i, has sum 0, so it is balanced.
            const length = i - firstAt.get(running)!;
            if (length > best) {
                best = length;
            }
        } else {
            // First time we see this sum: remember where. Never overwrite
            // it, because the earliest index gives the longest slice.
            firstAt.set(running, i);
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    public int findMaxLength(int[] nums) {
        // firstAt: running sum -> the FIRST index where we saw it
        Map<Integer, Integer> firstAt = new HashMap<>();
        // Running sum 0 is "seen" just before index 0 (at index -1).
        firstAt.put(0, -1);
        int running = 0;   // (number of 1s) - (number of 0s) so far
        int best = 0;      // longest balanced slice found so far
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int bit = nums[i];
            // Treat 1 as +1 and 0 as -1, so "equal counts" means "sum is 0".
            if (bit == 1) {
                running = running + 1;
            } else {
                running = running - 1;
            }
            if (firstAt.containsKey(running)) {
                // Same running sum as at index firstAt[running]: the slice
                // after that index, up to i, has sum 0, so it is balanced.
                int length = i - firstAt.get(running);
                if (length > best) {
                    best = length;
                }
            } else {
                // First time we see this sum: remember where. Never overwrite
                // it, because the earliest index gives the longest slice.
                firstAt.put(running, i);
            }
        }
        return best;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. first_at remembers the first index where each running sum appeared. first_at[0] = -1 says sum 0 happened "just before index 0".
  2. For each index, a 1 adds 1 to running and a 0 subtracts 1. So running = (ones so far) − (zeros so far).
  3. If this running was seen before at index first_at[running], the numbers between that index and i added up to 0: equal 0s and 1s. Its length is i - first_at[running]; keep it if it beats best.
  4. If it is new, store i as its first index. We never overwrite, because an earlier start means a longer slice.
  5. Return best.

Edge cases to test:

  • No balanced subarray, e.g. [0, 0, 0] → 0.
  • The whole array is balanced, e.g. [0, 1, 1, 0] → 4 (needs the seed {0: −1}).
  • Length 1 → always 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Medium 974. Subarray Sums Divisible by K Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays of nums whose sum is divisible by k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [4,5,0,-2,-3,1], k = 5
Output: 7
Explanation: There are 7 subarrays with a sum divisible by k = 5: [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], [5], [5, 0], [5, 0, -2, -3], [0], [0, -2, -3], [-2, -3]
Example 2
Input: nums = [5], k = 9
Output: 0

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 3 * 10⁴ · -10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴ · 2 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴

Hint 1

When is prefix[j] − prefix[i] divisible by k? Think about remainders.

Hint 2

Two prefixes with the same remainder mod k enclose a divisible slice. Count prefixes per remainder; each new prefix pairs with all earlier ones of the same remainder.

From brute force to the pattern: Sum every subarray and test % k: O(n²). A slice is divisible exactly when its two bounding prefix sums leave the same remainder, so you only need a count per remainder (an array of size k). Each prefix adds the count of earlier equal remainders: O(n + k).

Spot it: "divisible by k" means two prefixes with the same remainder mod k enclose a divisible slice. Count prefixes by remainder.

Approach:

  1. Keep counts of prefix remainders mod k, with remainder 0 seen once.
  2. For each number, update running = (running + x) % k.
  3. Every earlier prefix with the same remainder forms a divisible slice, so add its count, then increment it.
class Solution:
    def subarraysDivByK(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> int:
        # count_mod[r] = how many prefixes so far have remainder r (mod k).
        # [0] * k makes a list of k zeros.
        count_mod = [0] * k
        # The empty prefix has sum 0, so remainder 0 has been seen once.
        count_mod[0] = 1
        running = 0   # running sum, kept as a remainder mod k
        answer = 0
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            number = nums[i]
            # Python's % always gives a result from 0 to k - 1, even for
            # negative numbers, so it is safe to use as a list index.
            running = (running + number) % k
            # Every earlier prefix with the same remainder encloses a slice
            # whose sum is divisible by k.
            answer = answer + count_mod[running]
            # Count this prefix too, for later positions.
            count_mod[running] = count_mod[running] + 1
        return answer
function subarraysDivByK(nums: number[], k: number): number {
    // countMod[r] = how many prefixes so far have remainder r (mod k).
    const countMod: number[] = new Array(k).fill(0);
    // The empty prefix has sum 0, so remainder 0 has been seen once.
    countMod[0] = 1;
    let running = 0;   // running sum, kept as a remainder mod k
    let answer = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const number = nums[i];
        // In TypeScript, % keeps the sign (-1 % 5 is -1), so add k and take
        // % again to get a remainder from 0 to k - 1 that is safe as an index.
        running = (((running + number) % k) + k) % k;
        // Every earlier prefix with the same remainder encloses a slice
        // whose sum is divisible by k.
        answer = answer + countMod[running];
        // Count this prefix too, for later positions.
        countMod[running] = countMod[running] + 1;
    }
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    public int subarraysDivByK(int[] nums, int k) {
        // countMod[r] = how many prefixes so far have remainder r (mod k).
        // A new int array starts as all zeros.
        int[] countMod = new int[k];
        // The empty prefix has sum 0, so remainder 0 has been seen once.
        countMod[0] = 1;
        int running = 0;   // running sum, kept as a remainder mod k
        int answer = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int number = nums[i];
            // In Java, % keeps the sign (-1 % 5 is -1), so add k and take
            // % again to get a remainder from 0 to k - 1 that is safe as an index.
            running = ((running + number) % k + k) % k;
            // Every earlier prefix with the same remainder encloses a slice
            // whose sum is divisible by k.
            answer = answer + countMod[running];
            // Count this prefix too, for later positions.
            countMod[running] = countMod[running] + 1;
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. count_mod is a list with one counter per remainder 0..k−1. count_mod[0] = 1 counts the empty prefix.
  2. running holds the running sum, but we only keep its remainder mod k.
  3. For each number, update the remainder. Python's % never returns a negative number, so it is a safe index.
  4. Every earlier prefix with the same remainder forms a slice whose sum is divisible by k, so add count_mod[running] to answer.
  5. Then add 1 to count_mod[running] so later positions can pair with this prefix.

Dry run on the example nums = [4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], k = 5:

inumberrunning (remainder)added (count_mod[running] before)answercount_mod after
04400[1, 0, 0, 0, 1]
15411[1, 0, 0, 0, 2]
20423[1, 0, 0, 0, 3]
3-2203[1, 0, 1, 0, 3]
4-3436[1, 0, 1, 0, 4]
51017[2, 0, 1, 0, 4]

Result: 7. Notice -2: (4 + -2) % 5 is 2 in Python, never negative.

Edge cases to test:

  • Negative numbers: Python's % already returns a non-negative remainder (-1 % 5 == 4); in other languages add k.
  • Every element divisible by k, e.g. [5, 5], k = 5 → 3.
  • k = 1: every subarray counts, n(n + 1) / 2.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(k) space.

Medium 304. Range Sum Query 2D – Immutable Google Amazon Matrix

Problem: Design NumMatrix(matrix) with sumRegion(row1, col1, row2, col2), which returns the sum of the rectangle with top-left (row1, col1) and bottom-right (row2, col2) (inclusive). There can be up to 10⁴ queries, each must be O(1).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: ["NumMatrix", "sumRegion", "sumRegion", "sumRegion"] [[[[3, 0, 1, 4, 2], [5, 6, 3, 2, 1], [1, 2, 0, 1, 5], [4, 1, 0, 1, 7], [1, 0, 3, 0, 5]]], [2, 1, 4, 3], [1, 1, 2, 2], [1, 2, 2, 4]]
Output: [null, 8, 11, 12]
Explanation: NumMatrix numMatrix = new NumMatrix([[3, 0, 1, 4, 2], [5, 6, 3, 2, 1], [1, 2, 0, 1, 5], [4, 1, 0, 1, 7], [1, 0, 3, 0, 5]]); numMatrix.sumRegion(2, 1, 4, 3); // return 8 (i.e sum of the red rectangle) numMatrix.sumRegion(1, 1, 2, 2); // return 11 (i.e sum of the green rectangle) numMatrix.sumRegion(1, 2, 2, 4); // return 12 (i.e sum of the blue rectangle)

Constraints: m == matrix.length · n == matrix[i].length · 1 ≤ m, n ≤ 200 · -10⁴ ≤ matrix[i][j] ≤ 10⁴ · 0 ≤ row1 ≤ row2 < m · 0 ≤ col1 ≤ col2 < n · At most 10⁴ calls will be made to sumRegion.

Hint 1

Precompute P[r][c] = sum of everything above and to the left of (r, c). How do you build it from its neighbours?

Hint 2

A rectangle = big prefix − the strip above − the strip to the left + the corner you subtracted twice.

From brute force to the pattern: Adding up the rectangle cell by cell costs O(rows · cols) per query, too slow for many queries. A 2-D prefix sum spends O(rows · cols) once and then answers every query with four lookups (inclusion–exclusion).

Spot it: many rectangle-sum queries on a fixed grid. Use a 2-D prefix sum.

Inclusion–exclusion picture: big rectangle − top strip − left strip + the corner you subtracted twice.

Approach:

  1. Build P with one extra row and column of zeros.
  2. P[r+1][c+1] = cell + top + left − top-left (the overlap was added twice).
  3. Query = big − top strip − left strip + corner.
class NumMatrix:
    def __init__(self, matrix: List[List[int]]):
        rows = len(matrix)
        cols = len(matrix[0])
        # self.table has one extra row and one extra column of zeros.
        # self.table[row + 1][col + 1] = sum of the rectangle (0, 0) .. (row, col).
        self.table = []
        for row in range(rows + 1):
            # [0] * (cols + 1) makes one row of zeros
            self.table.append([0] * (cols + 1))
        for row in range(rows):
            for col in range(cols):
                cell = matrix[row][col]
                above = self.table[row][col + 1]    # rectangle ending one row up
                left = self.table[row + 1][col]     # rectangle ending one column left
                overlap = self.table[row][col]      # inside BOTH above and left
                # above + left counts the overlap twice, so take it away once
                self.table[row + 1][col + 1] = cell + above + left - overlap

    def sumRegion(self, row1: int, col1: int, row2: int, col2: int) -> int:
        big = self.table[row2 + 1][col2 + 1]       # (0, 0) .. (row2, col2)
        top_strip = self.table[row1][col2 + 1]     # all rows above row1
        left_strip = self.table[row2 + 1][col1]    # all columns left of col1
        corner = self.table[row1][col1]            # removed twice, add back once
        return big - top_strip - left_strip + corner
class NumMatrix {
    // table has one extra row and one extra column of zeros.
    // table[row + 1][col + 1] = sum of the rectangle (0, 0) .. (row, col).
    private table: number[][] = [];

    constructor(matrix: number[][]) {
        const rows = matrix.length;
        const cols = matrix[0].length;
        for (let row = 0; row <= rows; row++) {
            // one row of cols + 1 zeros
            this.table.push(new Array(cols + 1).fill(0));
        }
        for (let row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
            for (let col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                const cell = matrix[row][col];
                const above = this.table[row][col + 1];    // rectangle ending one row up
                const left = this.table[row + 1][col];     // rectangle ending one column left
                const overlap = this.table[row][col];      // inside BOTH above and left
                // above + left counts the overlap twice, so take it away once
                this.table[row + 1][col + 1] = cell + above + left - overlap;
            }
        }
    }

    sumRegion(row1: number, col1: number, row2: number, col2: number): number {
        const big = this.table[row2 + 1][col2 + 1];       // (0, 0) .. (row2, col2)
        const topStrip = this.table[row1][col2 + 1];      // all rows above row1
        const leftStrip = this.table[row2 + 1][col1];     // all columns left of col1
        const corner = this.table[row1][col1];            // removed twice, add back once
        return big - topStrip - leftStrip + corner;
    }
}
class NumMatrix {
    // table has one extra row and one extra column of zeros.
    // table[row + 1][col + 1] = sum of the rectangle (0, 0) .. (row, col).
    private int[][] table;

    public NumMatrix(int[][] matrix) {
        int rows = matrix.length;
        int cols = matrix[0].length;
        // a new int array starts as all zeros
        table = new int[rows + 1][cols + 1];
        for (int row = 0; row < rows; row++) {
            for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                int cell = matrix[row][col];
                int above = table[row][col + 1];    // rectangle ending one row up
                int left = table[row + 1][col];     // rectangle ending one column left
                int overlap = table[row][col];      // inside BOTH above and left
                // above + left counts the overlap twice, so take it away once
                table[row + 1][col + 1] = cell + above + left - overlap;
            }
        }
    }

    public int sumRegion(int row1, int col1, int row2, int col2) {
        int big = table[row2 + 1][col2 + 1];       // (0, 0) .. (row2, col2)
        int topStrip = table[row1][col2 + 1];      // all rows above row1
        int leftStrip = table[row2 + 1][col1];     // all columns left of col1
        int corner = table[row1][col1];            // removed twice, add back once
        return big - topStrip - leftStrip + corner;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. __init__ builds self.table with one extra row and column of zeros, one row at a time with append.
  2. For each cell, it reads the cell value, the rectangle sum just above (above), just to the left (left), and the diagonal one (overlap).
  3. above + left counts the overlap area twice, so the new value is cell + above + left - overlap.
  4. sumRegion reads four numbers from the table: the big rectangle from (0, 0) to the bottom-right corner, the strip above the query, the strip to its left, and the top-left corner.
  5. Big − top strip − left strip removes everything outside, but the corner was removed twice, so it is added back once.

Edge cases to test:

  • A single-cell region (row1 == row2, col1 == col2).
  • A region touching row 0 or column 0: the padded extra row/column of zeros avoids index −1.
  • Negative values in the matrix.

Complexity: build O(R·C), query O(1).

Hard 1074. Number of Submatrices That Sum to Target MatrixHash Map

Problem: Return the number of non-empty submatrices of matrix whose elements sum to target.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: matrix = [[0,1,0],[1,1,1],[0,1,0]], target = 0
Output: 4
Explanation: The four 1x1 submatrices that only contain 0.
Example 2
Input: matrix = [[1,-1],[-1,1]], target = 0
Output: 5
Explanation: The two 1x2 submatrices, plus the two 2x1 submatrices, plus the 2x2 submatrix.

Constraints: 1 ≤ matrix.length ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ matrix[0].length ≤ 100 · -1000 ≤ matrix[i][j] ≤ 1000 · -10^8 ≤ target ≤ 10^8

Hint 1

Fix a top row and a bottom row. What does the band between them look like if you add up each column?

Hint 2

Each band is a 1-D array of column sums, so count its subarrays with sum target using the LeetCode 560 hash-map trick.

From brute force to the pattern: Enumerating all submatrices is O(r² · c²) and summing each one adds more. Fixing the pair of rows reduces the problem to 1-D: squash the columns into sums, then count subarrays summing to target in O(c) with a prefix-sum map. Total O(r² · c).

Spot it: a 2-D version of #560. Fix a pair of rows (top, bottom). Squash the columns between them into a 1-D array of column sums, then run the #560 hash-map trick on it.

Approach:

  1. Pick a top row and extend the bottom row down one row at a time.
  2. Keep col[c] = sum of column c between top and bottom: a 1-D array.
  3. Run the #560 prefix + hash map count on col for target.
class Solution:
    def numSubmatrixSumTarget(self, matrix: List[List[int]], target: int) -> int:
        rows = len(matrix)
        cols = len(matrix[0])
        answer = 0
        for top in range(rows):
            # col_sums[col] = sum of column col from row top down to row bottom.
            col_sums = [0] * cols
            for bottom in range(top, rows):
                # Grow the band by one row: add row bottom into the column sums.
                for col in range(cols):
                    col_sums[col] = col_sums[col] + matrix[bottom][col]
                # col_sums is now a 1-D array. Count its slices that sum to
                # target with the problem 560 trick.
                seen = {}
                seen[0] = 1
                running = 0
                for col in range(cols):
                    running = running + col_sums[col]
                    needed = running - target
                    if needed in seen:
                        answer = answer + seen[needed]
                    if running not in seen:
                        seen[running] = 0
                    seen[running] = seen[running] + 1
        return answer
function numSubmatrixSumTarget(matrix: number[][], target: number): number {
    const rows = matrix.length;
    const cols = matrix[0].length;
    let answer = 0;
    for (let top = 0; top < rows; top++) {
        // colSums[col] = sum of column col from row top down to row bottom.
        const colSums: number[] = new Array(cols).fill(0);
        for (let bottom = top; bottom < rows; bottom++) {
            // Grow the band by one row: add row bottom into the column sums.
            for (let col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                colSums[col] = colSums[col] + matrix[bottom][col];
            }
            // colSums is now a 1-D array. Count its slices that sum to
            // target with the problem 560 trick.
            const seen = new Map<number, number>();
            seen.set(0, 1);
            let running = 0;
            for (let col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                running = running + colSums[col];
                const needed = running - target;
                if (seen.has(needed)) {
                    answer = answer + seen.get(needed)!;
                }
                seen.set(running, (seen.get(running) ?? 0) + 1);
            }
        }
    }
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    public int numSubmatrixSumTarget(int[][] matrix, int target) {
        int rows = matrix.length;
        int cols = matrix[0].length;
        int answer = 0;
        for (int top = 0; top < rows; top++) {
            // colSums[col] = sum of column col from row top down to row bottom.
            int[] colSums = new int[cols];
            for (int bottom = top; bottom < rows; bottom++) {
                // Grow the band by one row: add row bottom into the column sums.
                for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                    colSums[col] = colSums[col] + matrix[bottom][col];
                }
                // colSums is now a 1-D array. Count its slices that sum to
                // target with the problem 560 trick.
                Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
                seen.put(0, 1);
                int running = 0;
                for (int col = 0; col < cols; col++) {
                    running = running + colSums[col];
                    int needed = running - target;
                    if (seen.containsKey(needed)) {
                        answer = answer + seen.get(needed);
                    }
                    seen.put(running, seen.getOrDefault(running, 0) + 1);
                }
            }
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The outer loop picks a top row and starts a fresh col_sums list of zeros.
  2. The middle loop moves bottom down one row at a time and adds that row into col_sums. Now col_sums[col] is the sum of column col between top and bottom.
  3. Any sub-matrix that uses exactly rows top..bottom is a slice of col_sums. So we run the problem 560 code on col_sums with target.
  4. That inner part keeps seen and running exactly like 560, adding seen[needed] to answer each time.
  5. After every pair of rows has been tried, answer is the total count.

Dry run on the example matrix = [[0, 1, 0], [1, 1, 1], [0, 1, 0]], target = 0:

topbottomcol_sumsslices of col_sums with sum 0answer

Result: 4: the four single-cell zeros in the corners.

Edge cases to test:

  • A single cell equal to target.
  • target = 0 with zeros and negatives (the {0: 1} seed matters).
  • One row or one column: it degenerates to plain LeetCode 560.

Complexity: O(R²·C) time, O(C) space. Make R the smaller dimension.

8. Common mistakes

Off-by-oneWithout the leading 0 you'll write prefix[r] - prefix[l-1] and crash at l = 0. Always pad.
Forgetting seen[0] = 1This misses subarrays that start at index 0.
Updating the map before countingThen you count a zero-length slice when k = 0.
For "longest", store the first index; for "count", store frequenciesMixing these up is the #1 bug in 525-style problems.

9. Self-check quiz

Count subarrays of [3, -1, 4, -2, 2] that sum to 4.

Negative numbers break the "shrink when too big" logic of Sliding Window. Prefix Sum doesn't care about signs.

Longest subarray with sum ≤ S, where every value is positive.

All values are positive, so the window sum only grows when you expand and only shrinks when you contract. That's Sliding Window, in O(1) space.

With a 0-padded prefix array, the sum of nums[l..r] is…

"Right plus one minus left."

Easy 303. Range Sum Query – Immutable Start here Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Given a fixed array, answer many sumRange(left, right) calls (inclusive) quickly.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: ["NumArray", "sumRange", "sumRange", "sumRange"] [[[-2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1]], [0, 2], [2, 5], [0, 5]]
Output: [null, 1, -1, -3]
Explanation: NumArray numArray = new NumArray([-2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1]); numArray.sumRange(0, 2); // return (-2) + 0 + 3 = 1 numArray.sumRange(2, 5); // return 3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -1 numArray.sumRange(0, 5); // return (-2) + 0 + 3 + (-5) + 2 + (-1) = -3

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁴ · -10⁵ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ left ≤ right < nums.length · At most 10⁴ calls will be made to sumRange.

Hint 1

Many queries on the same array: what can you precompute once?

Hint 2

With prefix[i] = sum of the first i numbers, the sum of left..right is a single subtraction.

From brute force to the pattern: Summing nums[left..right] per query is O(n) each, so q queries cost O(n · q). Building the prefix array once in O(n) makes every query O(1).

Spot it: "many queries" on an array that never changes. That's textbook Prefix Sum.

  1. In the constructor, build prefix with a leading 0.
  2. For each query, return prefix[right+1] − prefix[left].
class NumArray:
    def __init__(self, nums: List[int]):
        # self.prefix[i] = sum of the first i numbers.
        # It starts with 0, which means "the sum of nothing".
        self.prefix = [0]
        running_total = 0
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            running_total = running_total + nums[i]
            # store the running total after element i
            self.prefix.append(running_total)

    def sumRange(self, left: int, right: int) -> int:
        # "right plus one minus left"
        return self.prefix[right + 1] - self.prefix[left]
class NumArray {
    // prefix[i] = sum of the first i numbers.
    // It starts with 0, which means "the sum of nothing".
    private prefix: number[] = [0];

    constructor(nums: number[]) {
        let runningTotal = 0;
        for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            runningTotal = runningTotal + nums[i];
            // store the running total after element i
            this.prefix.push(runningTotal);
        }
    }

    sumRange(left: number, right: number): number {
        // "right plus one minus left"
        return this.prefix[right + 1] - this.prefix[left];
    }
}
class NumArray {
    // prefix[i] = sum of the first i numbers.
    // prefix[0] = 0 means "the sum of nothing".
    private int[] prefix;

    public NumArray(int[] nums) {
        prefix = new int[nums.length + 1];
        int runningTotal = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            runningTotal = runningTotal + nums[i];
            // store the running total after element i
            prefix[i + 1] = runningTotal;
        }
    }

    public int sumRange(int left, int right) {
        // "right plus one minus left"
        return prefix[right + 1] - prefix[left];
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. __init__ starts self.prefix as [0] (sum of nothing) and keeps a running_total.
  2. For each number, it adds the number to running_total and appends the new total. So self.prefix[i] is the sum of the first i numbers.
  3. sumRange returns self.prefix[right + 1] - self.prefix[left]: everything through right, minus everything before left.

inums[i]running_totalself.prefix after
0-2-2[0, -2]
10-2[0, -2, -2]
231[0, -2, -2, 1]
3-5-4[0, -2, -2, 1, -4]
42-2[0, -2, -2, 1, -4, -2]
5-1-3[0, -2, -2, 1, -4, -2, -3]
querycomputationresult
sumRange(0, 2)prefix[3] - prefix[0] = 1 - 01
sumRange(2, 5)prefix[6] - prefix[2] = -3 - -2-1
sumRange(0, 5)prefix[6] - prefix[0] = -3 - 0-3

Edge cases to test:

  • left == right (a single element).
  • The whole array (left = 0, right = n − 1): this is why prefix has n + 1 entries.
  • Negative numbers.

Complexity: build O(n), each query O(1), space O(n).

Medium 238. Product of Array Except Self Start here Google Meta Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Return answer[i] = product of every element except nums[i], without using division, in O(n).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ · Video walkthrough ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [1,2,3,4]
Output: [24,12,8,6]
Example 2
Input: nums = [-1,1,0,-3,3]
Output: [0,0,9,0,0]

Constraints: 2 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · -30 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 30 · The input is generated such that answer[i] is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.

Hint 1

answer[i] = (product of everything to the left of i) × (product of everything to the right).

Hint 2

Build the left products in one pass, then sweep from the right with a running product. No division needed.

From brute force to the pattern: For each i, multiply all other elements: O(n²). Dividing the total product by nums[i] breaks on zeros and is forbidden. Prefix products from the left and suffix products from the right give each answer in O(1), so O(n) overall.

Spot it: "everything except i" = (everything to the left of i) × (everything to the right of i). That's a prefix product times a suffix product.

  1. Left pass: answer[i] = product of nums[0..i-1], starting from 1.
  2. Right pass: keep a running suffix product and multiply it into answer[i] while walking from the end.
  3. No extra arrays needed: the output array holds the prefix products.
class Solution:
    def productExceptSelf(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        size = len(nums)
        # [1] * size makes a list of size ones (1 is the "empty product")
        answer = [1] * size
        # Pass 1, left to right: answer[i] = product of everything LEFT of i.
        left_product = 1
        for i in range(size):
            answer[i] = left_product
            left_product = left_product * nums[i]
        # Pass 2, right to left: multiply in the product of everything RIGHT of i.
        right_product = 1
        i = size - 1
        while i >= 0:
            answer[i] = answer[i] * right_product
            right_product = right_product * nums[i]
            i = i - 1
        return answer
function productExceptSelf(nums: number[]): number[] {
    const size = nums.length;
    // a list of size ones (1 is the "empty product")
    const answer: number[] = new Array(size).fill(1);
    // Pass 1, left to right: answer[i] = product of everything LEFT of i.
    let leftProduct = 1;
    for (let i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        answer[i] = leftProduct;
        leftProduct = leftProduct * nums[i];
    }
    // Pass 2, right to left: multiply in the product of everything RIGHT of i.
    let rightProduct = 1;
    let i = size - 1;
    while (i >= 0) {
        answer[i] = answer[i] * rightProduct;
        rightProduct = rightProduct * nums[i];
        i = i - 1;
    }
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] productExceptSelf(int[] nums) {
        int size = nums.length;
        int[] answer = new int[size];
        // Pass 1, left to right: answer[i] = product of everything LEFT of i.
        // It starts at 1, the "empty product".
        int leftProduct = 1;
        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            answer[i] = leftProduct;
            leftProduct = leftProduct * nums[i];
        }
        // Pass 2, right to left: multiply in the product of everything RIGHT of i.
        int rightProduct = 1;
        int i = size - 1;
        while (i >= 0) {
            answer[i] = answer[i] * rightProduct;
            rightProduct = rightProduct * nums[i];
            i = i - 1;
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. size is how many numbers there are. answer starts as a list of size ones.
  2. Pass 1 walks left to right. Before multiplying, it stores left_product (the product of everything left of i) into answer[i], then multiplies nums[i] into left_product.
  3. Pass 2 walks right to left with a while loop: i starts at size - 1 (the last index) and goes down by 1 until it passes 0.
  4. At each step it multiplies answer[i] by right_product (the product of everything right of i), then multiplies nums[i] into right_product.
  5. Now answer[i] = (left product) × (right product) = everything except nums[i], with no division.

Dry run on the example nums = [1, 2, 3, 4]:

passinums[i]product after this stepanswer
1 (left to right)01left_product = 1[1, 1, 1, 1]
1 (left to right)12left_product = 2[1, 1, 1, 1]
1 (left to right)23left_product = 6[1, 1, 2, 1]
1 (left to right)34left_product = 24[1, 1, 2, 6]
2 (right to left)34right_product = 4[1, 1, 2, 6]
2 (right to left)23right_product = 12[1, 1, 8, 6]
2 (right to left)12right_product = 24[1, 12, 8, 6]
2 (right to left)01right_product = 24[24, 12, 8, 6]

Result: [24, 12, 8, 6].

Edge cases to test:

  • One zero, e.g. [1, 2, 0, 4] → only index 2 is non-zero.
  • Two zeros → every answer is 0.
  • Negative numbers, e.g. [-1, 1, 0, -3, 3].

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (not counting the output).

Medium 523. Continuous Subarray Sum Google Microsoft ArrayHash Map

Problem: Return true if there is a subarray of length ≥ 2 whose sum is a multiple of k.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [23,2,4,6,7], k = 6
Output: true
Explanation: [2, 4] is a continuous subarray of size 2 whose elements sum up to 6.
Example 2
Input: nums = [23,2,6,4,7], k = 6
Output: true
Explanation: [23, 2, 6, 4, 7] is an continuous subarray of size 5 whose elements sum up to 42. 42 is a multiple of 6 because 42 = 7 * 6 and 7 is an integer.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 0 ≤ sum(nums[i]) ≤ 2³¹ - 1 · 1 ≤ k ≤ 2³¹ - 1

Hint 1

Like LeetCode 974, compare prefix remainders mod k. What's different here?

Hint 2

The subarray must have length at least 2, so store the first index of each remainder and check the distance.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every subarray of length ≥ 2 is O(n²). Equal remainders mod k mean the slice between them is a multiple of k; remembering where each remainder first appeared lets one pass check the length condition in O(1).

Spot it: "multiple of k" = same remainder trick as #974. "Length ≥ 2" means you must store the first index of each remainder and check the distance.

  1. Keep first_at = {0: -1}: remainder 0 is seen "before" index 0.
  2. Walk with running = (running + x) % k.
  3. If this remainder was seen at index j and i − j ≥ 2, return true.
  4. Otherwise record the remainder only the first time you see it, to keep the longest distance.
class Solution:
    def checkSubarraySum(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> bool:
        # first_at: remainder -> earliest index where the running sum had it
        first_at = {}
        first_at[0] = -1   # remainder 0 is "seen" just before index 0
        running = 0
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            number = nums[i]
            running = (running + number) % k
            if running in first_at:
                # Same remainder as at index first_at[running]: the slice after
                # that index, up to i, has a sum that is a multiple of k.
                length = i - first_at[running]
                if length >= 2:
                    return True
            else:
                # Never overwrite: the earliest index gives the longest slice.
                first_at[running] = i
        return False
function checkSubarraySum(nums: number[], k: number): boolean {
    // firstAt: remainder -> earliest index where the running sum had it
    const firstAt = new Map<number, number>();
    firstAt.set(0, -1);   // remainder 0 is "seen" just before index 0
    let running = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        const number = nums[i];
        running = (running + number) % k;   // the numbers are never negative here
        if (firstAt.has(running)) {
            // Same remainder as at index firstAt[running]: the slice after
            // that index, up to i, has a sum that is a multiple of k.
            const length = i - firstAt.get(running)!;
            if (length >= 2) {
                return true;
            }
        } else {
            // Never overwrite: the earliest index gives the longest slice.
            firstAt.set(running, i);
        }
    }
    return false;
}
class Solution {
    public boolean checkSubarraySum(int[] nums, int k) {
        // firstAt: remainder -> earliest index where the running sum had it
        Map<Integer, Integer> firstAt = new HashMap<>();
        firstAt.put(0, -1);   // remainder 0 is "seen" just before index 0
        int running = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            int number = nums[i];
            running = (running + number) % k;   // the numbers are never negative here
            if (firstAt.containsKey(running)) {
                // Same remainder as at index firstAt[running]: the slice after
                // that index, up to i, has a sum that is a multiple of k.
                int length = i - firstAt.get(running);
                if (length >= 2) {
                    return true;
                }
            } else {
                // Never overwrite: the earliest index gives the longest slice.
                firstAt.put(running, i);
            }
        }
        return false;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. first_at maps a remainder to the earliest index where the running sum had it. first_at[0] = -1 covers slices that start at index 0.
  2. Each step adds the number and keeps only the remainder mod k.
  3. If that remainder was seen before, the slice between has a sum that is a multiple of k. Its length is i - first_at[running]; if that is at least 2, return True.
  4. If the remainder is new, store the index. Never overwrite, so we always measure from the earliest index.
  5. If the loop ends with no success, return False.

Dry run on the example nums = [23, 2, 4, 6, 7], k = 6:

inumberrunning (remainder)what happensresult
0235new remainder, store first_at[5] = 0keep going
121new remainder, store first_at[1] = 1keep going
245seen at index 0, length 2 >= 2return True

Result: True: the slice [2, 4] (indices 1..2) sums to 6.

Edge cases to test:

  • [0, 0] with any k → True (0 is a multiple of every k).
  • A single element that is a multiple of k, e.g. [6], k = 6 → False (length 1).
  • Seeding {0: −1} so a valid prefix starting at index 0 is found.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(min(n, k)) space.

Medium 437. Path Sum III Google Amazon Binary TreeHash Map

Problem: Count downward paths in a binary tree (from any node to any descendant) whose values sum to targetSum.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: root = [10,5,-3,3,2,null,11,3,-2,null,1], targetSum = 8
Output: 3
Explanation: The paths that sum to 8 are shown.
Example 2
Input: root = [5,4,8,11,null,13,4,7,2,null,null,5,1], targetSum = 22
Output: 3

Constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 1000]. · -10⁹ ≤ Node.val ≤ 10⁹ · -1000 ≤ targetSum ≤ 1000

Hint 1

Along any root-to-node path, a downward path with sum target is a difference of two prefix sums on that path.

Hint 2

DFS with a count map of the prefix sums on the current path; add the node's sum on the way down and remove it on the way back up.

From brute force to the pattern: Starting a DFS from every node and following every downward path is O(n²) on a skewed tree. Treating each root-to-node path like an array, the prefix-sum hash map counts matching paths ending at each node in O(1), so O(n) total.

Spot it: a root-to-node path is just an array. Count "subarrays with sum = target" along it, which is #560, done during a DFS.

  1. DFS from the root, carrying the running sum from the root to the current node.
  2. At each node, add seen[running − target] to the answer.
  3. Add running to seen, recurse into both children, then remove it on the way back (backtrack). This keeps only the current path's prefixes in the map.
class Solution:
    def pathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode], targetSum: int) -> int:
        # self.seen: running sum from the root -> how many nodes on the
        # CURRENT path (root down to here) have that running sum.
        self.seen = {}
        self.seen[0] = 1          # the empty path above the root
        self.target = targetSum
        return self.count_paths(root, 0)

    # Helper method (a separate method instead of a nested function).
    # Returns how many good paths end somewhere in the subtree of node.
    def count_paths(self, node, running):
        if node is None:
            return 0
        running = running + node.val
        # Paths that END at this node: earlier prefixes equal to running - target.
        needed = running - self.target
        count = 0
        if needed in self.seen:
            count = self.seen[needed]
        # Make this prefix visible to the nodes below.
        if running not in self.seen:
            self.seen[running] = 0
        self.seen[running] = self.seen[running] + 1
        count = count + self.count_paths(node.left, running)
        count = count + self.count_paths(node.right, running)
        # Backtrack: we are leaving this node, so remove its prefix again.
        self.seen[running] = self.seen[running] - 1
        return count
function pathSum(root: TreeNode | null, targetSum: number): number {
    // seen: running sum from the root -> how many nodes on the
    // CURRENT path (root down to here) have that running sum.
    const seen = new Map<number, number>();
    seen.set(0, 1);          // the empty path above the root

    // Returns how many good paths end somewhere in the subtree of node.
    function countPaths(node: TreeNode | null, running: number): number {
        if (node === null) {
            return 0;
        }
        running = running + node.val;
        // Paths that END at this node: earlier prefixes equal to running - target.
        const needed = running - targetSum;
        let count = seen.get(needed) ?? 0;
        // Make this prefix visible to the nodes below.
        seen.set(running, (seen.get(running) ?? 0) + 1);
        count = count + countPaths(node.left, running);
        count = count + countPaths(node.right, running);
        // Backtrack: we are leaving this node, so remove its prefix again.
        seen.set(running, seen.get(running)! - 1);
        return count;
    }

    return countPaths(root, 0);
}
class Solution {
    // seen: running sum from the root -> how many nodes on the
    // CURRENT path (root down to here) have that running sum.
    // Sums can pass the int range, so they are long.
    private Map<Long, Integer> seen;
    private int target;

    public int pathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
        seen = new HashMap<>();
        seen.put(0L, 1);          // the empty path above the root
        target = targetSum;
        return countPaths(root, 0L);
    }

    // Returns how many good paths end somewhere in the subtree of node.
    private int countPaths(TreeNode node, long running) {
        if (node == null) {
            return 0;
        }
        running = running + node.val;
        // Paths that END at this node: earlier prefixes equal to running - target.
        long needed = running - target;
        int count = seen.getOrDefault(needed, 0);
        // Make this prefix visible to the nodes below.
        seen.put(running, seen.getOrDefault(running, 0) + 1);
        count = count + countPaths(node.left, running);
        count = count + countPaths(node.right, running);
        // Backtrack: we are leaving this node, so remove its prefix again.
        seen.put(running, seen.get(running) - 1);
        return count;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. pathSum sets up shared state on self: the seen dictionary (seeded with {0: 1}) and the target. Then it calls the helper on the root with running sum 0.
  2. count_paths returns 0 for a missing child (node is None).
  3. Otherwise it adds node.val to running, the sum from the root down to this node.
  4. Paths that end here and sum to the target start right after an ancestor whose running sum was running - target. self.seen[needed] says how many such ancestors there are.
  5. It records running in self.seen so the children can use it, then adds the counts from the left and right subtrees.
  6. Before returning, it subtracts 1 from self.seen[running] (backtracking), so sibling branches do not see this node's total.

Dry run on the example root = [10, 5, -3, 3, 2, null, 11, 3, -2, null, 1], targetSum = 8. Rows are in DFS visit order (node, then its left subtree, then its right subtree):

visit nodecurrent pathrunningneeded = running - 8paths ending hereseen on the path (after adding)
10101020{0: 1, 10: 1}
510 → 51570{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1}
310 → 5 → 318101{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1, 18: 1}
310 → 5 → 3 → 321130{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1, 18: 1, 21: 1}
-210 → 5 → 3 → -21680{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1, 18: 1, 16: 1}
210 → 5 → 21790{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1, 17: 1}
110 → 5 → 2 → 118101{0: 1, 10: 1, 15: 1, 18: 1, 17: 1}
-310 → -37-10{0: 1, 10: 1, 7: 1}
1110 → -3 → 1118101{0: 1, 10: 1, 18: 1, 7: 1}

Result: 3: the paths 5 → 3, 5 → 2 → 1 and -3 → 11. Notice how seen only ever holds the totals of the current path, thanks to the backtracking step.

Edge cases to test:

  • Negative values, so a path can still match after the sum overshoots.
  • targetSum = 0 with zero-valued nodes.
  • An empty tree → 0.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space (h = tree height).

Medium 1590. Make Sum Divisible by P Google ArrayHash Map

Problem: Remove the shortest subarray (it may be empty, but you can't remove the whole array) so the sum of what remains is divisible by p. Return its length, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: nums = [3,1,4,2], p = 6
Output: 1
Explanation: The sum of the elements in nums is 10, which is not divisible by 6. We can remove the subarray [4], and the sum of the remaining elements is 6, which is divisible by 6.
Example 2
Input: nums = [6,3,5,2], p = 9
Output: 2
Explanation: We cannot remove a single element to get a sum divisible by 9. The best way is to remove the subarray [5,2], leaving us with [6,3] with sum 9.

Constraints: 1 ≤ nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁹ · 1 ≤ p ≤ 10⁹

Hint 1

Let need = sum(nums) % p. You must remove a subarray whose sum has remainder need.

Hint 2

Remember the latest index of each prefix remainder; at index j look for the remainder (prefix − need) mod p.

From brute force to the pattern: Trying every subarray to remove and re-checking the rest is O(n²) or worse. In remainder terms, you need the shortest slice with sum ≡ need (mod p): a prefix-remainder map storing the latest index finds the shortest one ending at each j in O(1).

Spot it: the removed slice must have sum % p == total % p. That's a remainder lookup, and because it asks for the shortest, store the latest index of each remainder.

  1. need = total % p. If it's 0, return 0.
  2. Walk with running % p. A slice (j, i] works when (running_i − running_j) % p == need, i.e. running_j ≡ running_i − need.
  3. Look that up in last_at and keep the minimum length. Always overwrite last_at[running] with the newest index.
  4. If the best length is the whole array, return −1.
class Solution:
    def minSubarray(self, nums: List[int], divisor: int) -> int:
        # (LeetCode calls the divisor p.)
        # Add up all the numbers with a plain loop.
        total = 0
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            total = total + nums[i]
        # The removed slice must have this same remainder.
        need = total % divisor
        if need == 0:
            return 0       # already divisible: remove nothing
        # last_at: remainder -> LATEST index where a prefix had that remainder
        last_at = {}
        last_at[0] = -1    # the empty prefix
        running = 0
        best = len(nums)   # means "not found yet" (removing everything is not allowed)
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            running = (running + nums[i]) % divisor
            # An earlier prefix with remainder want encloses a slice whose
            # remainder is need.
            want = (running - need) % divisor
            if want in last_at:
                length = i - last_at[want]
                if length < best:
                    best = length
            # Always overwrite: the most recent index gives the shortest slice.
            last_at[running] = i
        if best < len(nums):
            return best
        else:
            return -1
function minSubarray(nums: number[], p: number): number {
    // Add up all the numbers with a plain loop.
    let total = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        total = total + nums[i];
    }
    // The removed slice must have this same remainder.
    const need = total % p;
    if (need === 0) {
        return 0;       // already divisible: remove nothing
    }
    // lastAt: remainder -> LATEST index where a prefix had that remainder
    const lastAt = new Map<number, number>();
    lastAt.set(0, -1);    // the empty prefix
    let running = 0;
    let best = nums.length;   // means "not found yet" (removing everything is not allowed)
    for (let i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
        running = (running + nums[i]) % p;
        // An earlier prefix with remainder want encloses a slice whose
        // remainder is need. (+ p keeps the result from going negative.)
        const want = (running - need + p) % p;
        if (lastAt.has(want)) {
            const length = i - lastAt.get(want)!;
            if (length < best) {
                best = length;
            }
        }
        // Always overwrite: the most recent index gives the shortest slice.
        lastAt.set(running, i);
    }
    if (best < nums.length) {
        return best;
    } else {
        return -1;
    }
}
class Solution {
    public int minSubarray(int[] nums, int p) {
        // Add up all the numbers with a plain loop.
        // The total can pass the int range, so it is a long.
        long total = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            total = total + nums[i];
        }
        // The removed slice must have this same remainder.
        int need = (int) (total % p);
        if (need == 0) {
            return 0;       // already divisible: remove nothing
        }
        // lastAt: remainder -> LATEST index where a prefix had that remainder
        Map<Integer, Integer> lastAt = new HashMap<>();
        lastAt.put(0, -1);    // the empty prefix
        int running = 0;
        int best = nums.length;   // means "not found yet" (removing everything is not allowed)
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            running = (running + nums[i]) % p;
            // An earlier prefix with remainder want encloses a slice whose
            // remainder is need. (+ p keeps the result from going negative.)
            int want = (running - need + p) % p;
            if (lastAt.containsKey(want)) {
                int length = i - lastAt.get(want);
                if (length < best) {
                    best = length;
                }
            }
            // Always overwrite: the most recent index gives the shortest slice.
            lastAt.put(running, i);
        }
        if (best < nums.length) {
            return best;
        } else {
            return -1;
        }
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A plain loop adds up total. need = total % divisor is the remainder the removed slice must have. If it is 0, nothing needs removing.
  2. last_at maps a remainder to the latest index with that prefix remainder, seeded with {0: -1}.
  3. best starts at len(nums), which means "nothing valid found" because removing the whole array is not allowed.
  4. Each step updates running (a remainder) and computes want = (running - need) % divisor: the remainder an earlier prefix must have so that the slice in between has remainder need.
  5. If want is in last_at, the slice length is i - last_at[want]; keep it if shorter.
  6. Always overwrite last_at[running] = i: a more recent start gives a shorter slice.
  7. At the end, return best if it was improved, otherwise −1.
